title: How 3 extra bits fix any error (Hamming, 1950)
description:
Sending your 4 bits three times takes 12 bits and lets a majority vote fix any one flipped bit. Richard Hamming's code does the same job with 7: put the 4 data bits in the overlaps of three circles, then give each circle one extra bit so it holds an even number of ones. If a bit flips, the circles that come out odd point to the only spot inside exactly those circles, so you flip it back. Three yes-or-no checks give 8 answers (no error, or one of 7 spots), which is why 3 extra bits are enough. Hamming built it at Bell Labs after errors kept killing his weekend jobs on the Model V relay computer, and published it in 1950.

Numbers checked in code: all 16 messages with every single flipped bit decode correctly (and 100,000 random trials), and each of the 7 flips gives a different pattern of odd circles. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_code

beats.say: Copy it three times: 12 bits. Hamming needed 7.
Same job: one bit flips on the way, and you still get your message back.
Bell Labs, the late 1940s. Richard Hamming's machine could spot errors, but not fix them, so his weekend jobs kept dying.
Take your 4 bits, one, zero, one, one, and drop them into the overlaps of three circles.
Fill each circle's empty spot so it holds an even number of ones. That's 3 extra bits, 7 in all.
Now one bit flips. You don't know which. The circles do.
Two circles come out odd. Only one spot sits inside exactly those two. Flip it back.
Three yes or no checks give 8 answers: no error, or one of 7 spots. That's why 3 extra bits cover all 7.
